full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN, with medium confidence.**

**1. Model family.** This is a coevolving (adaptive-network) opinion model with two states. Each node takes the local majority state of its neighbours, and discordant links are cut and rewired to a random node of the same state (rewire-to-same). The variants add either noise (`FLIP`, p=0.001) or very high rewiring rates. The usual names are the "adaptive/coevolving voter model" and, for the majority-rule version, the "majority-preference + minority-avoidance" model.

**2. Specific behaviour and sources.**
- **Closest match to this exact rule pair.** The paper "Coevolutionary dynamics of opinions and networks: From diversity to uniformity" (Phys. Rev. E 78, 016104) studies the same two rules. Under majority preference, individuals adopt the majority opinion among their neighbours. Under minority avoidance, individuals break the link to a neighbour with a different, minority opinion and rewire to a same-opinion node, either a neighbour's neighbour or a random one. I only saw the abstract, so I have not checked what it reports about fragmentation. Its model is also not identical to yours (see section 4).
- **Earliest clear source for rewire-to-same coevolution.** Holme & Newman 2006 (PRE 74, 056108). Their model has a single parameter balancing the two processes and undergoes a continuous phase transition, from a regime in which opinions are arbitrarily diverse to one in which most individuals hold the same opinion. In the final state, all edges join individuals of the same opinion, so the population splits into single-opinion components. This is the consensus-versus-fragmentation behaviour your run passes the test for.
- **Review and related work.**
  - Durrett et al., "Graph fission in an evolving voter model" (PNAS 2012), studies rewire-to-same. It finds a phase transition similar to Holme and Newman's.
  - Nardini, Kozma & Barrat (PRL 100, 158701) report that for fast rewiring the network breaks into typically two separate connected components, each with a local consensus.
  - The Gross & Sayama group's review "Adaptive Dynamical Networks" (arXiv 2304.05652) covers the adaptive voter model: a fragmented state in which all links connecting agents of different opinions have been cut.
  - A recent paper (arXiv 2511.15043) argues that fragmentation is independent of the node dynamics employed and just a consequence of extreme homophilic rewiring. That covers your majority-rule node dynamics as well.
- **Majority rule with rewiring, in a link-state version.** Raducha/San Miguel-group work (arXiv 1403.6106) finds that depending on the relative rates of majority rule and rewiring, the system ends in either a one-component network or a network fragmented into two components with opposite states.
- **Noise variants.** Diakonova, Eguíluz & San Miguel, "Noise in coevolving networks" (PRE 92, 032803), is the closest match to your `FLIP` rule programs. Noise on all nodes destroys the absorbing-fragmentation transition and gives bimodal magnetisation and dynamic fragmentation. Noise on a fraction of nodes keeps the transitions but adds shattered fragmentation, with isolated nodes and one or two giant components.
  - Your fingerprint has many components (n_components 1.39), a large but not complete giant component (0.77) and some type entropy. That looks like this shattered or dynamic fragmentation rather than a clean two-component split.
  - A follow-up, Raducha & San Miguel (Sci. Rep. 2020), also reports dynamic fragmentation, where noise in node states and rewiring keeps components being reconnected and disconnected.

**3. Verification.** Every source above appeared in search results, and I read the abstracts or text snippets. I did not read full texts. In particular, I did not check the PRE 78 016104 results section or the Diakonova paper's exact parameter regimes.

**4. Differences from the literature, and whether they matter.**
- Your updates are synchronous and applied to all nodes, with rewiring at probability p per step. The literature mostly uses asynchronous updates, one node or edge at a time.
- The majority rule is the deterministic local majority, not voter copying.
- Rewiring goes to a uniformly random same-type node.
- The odd fingerprint is probably a finite-size effect (200 nodes, mean degree 4) combined with these synchronous, noisy dynamics. I would expect it to be a quantitative change rather than a new phenomenon.
- This is a judgment call: I found no paper that tests this exact synchronous variant.

**5. Confidence.** Medium. Fragmentation under rewire-to-same coevolution, the majority-rule version, and noise-induced dynamic or shattered fragmentation are all documented. The residual uncertainty is that I did not find a paper using this exact synchronous majority-plus-rewire-plus-flip combination at N=200. I also did not test whether the unusual fingerprint matches the shattered-fragmentation regime.
